artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

artifacts.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

artifacts.synopsis: TE Aaron Myers appealed his conviction on charges of maltreatment of his wife and fits of anger by Illiana Presbytery; the SJC denied the appeal and upheld all four specifications of error arguments raised by the appellant, affirming the indefinite suspension from office and suspension from the sacraments.

artifacts.title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

artifacts.synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

artifacts.synopsis: Arizona Presbytery deposed TE Evans under BCO 38-1 without properly securing his approval of the full statement of facts, as the Investigative Committee's report added additional adverse facts he had not seen or approved. The SJC sustained the complaints of Evans and Pitts et al., annulled the deposition, and remanded the matter to AZP for action consistent with BCO 38-1 requirements; a lengthy concurring opinion by RE Donahoe extensively analyzed BCO 38-1 confession procedures.

artifacts.title: Malone v. Metro NY
artifacts.synopsis: Malone challenged Presbytery’s approval of a commission’s judgment and indefinite suspension imposed without process. The SJC sustained the complaint in part and vacated the judgment and censure: the commission had authority only to investigate, and Malone’s general acknowledgments neither confessed specific charges nor showed intent to waive process under BCO 38-1. Presbytery could begin anew under proper procedures. The SJC rejected Malone’s claim that suggested steps evidencing repentance improperly bound him, treating them as noncompulsory pastoral advice.

artifacts.title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

artifacts.synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

artifacts.synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s refusal to decide his guilt or innocence and its failure to return charges after his Session suspended him from the sacraments without trial or confession. The SJC sustained the complaint on the remand issue: rescission of the censure did not dispose of pending charges, so Presbytery had to rehear the complaint and require the Session either to institute proper process or dismiss them. It declined to determine guilt without a trial record and rejected the claim that the censure’s prescribed form willfully took the Lord’s name in vain.

artifacts.synopsis: A member suspended from the Lord's Table appealed after Presbytery let the Session resume her trial and failed to lift all suspensions. The SJC sustained the appeal, finding the Session's premature censure, truncated trial, and prosecutor-judge conflict manifested prejudice and made a fair trial impossible. It set aside all judgments and censures, treated the November 13, 2003 communion letter as non-censuring advice, and did not remand.

artifacts.synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

artifacts.synopsis: A church member appealed convictions and excommunication arising from vulgar statements to two patients, challenging the lack of pretrial reconciliation, recusals, the prosecutor’s participation in deliberations, and Presbytery procedure. The SJC left guilt intact and denied a new trial, though it held that a prosecutor may not deliberate as a judge. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. It remanded only to impose indefinite suspension from the Sacraments and conditions pending satisfactory evidence of repentance.

artifacts.synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s affirmance of his excommunication, contending that SJC Case 97-9 had reversed his four guilty verdicts and precluded increased censure. The SJC did not sustain either issue. Case 97-9 had reversed only the original censure, leaving guilt intact. Because the offender bore the burden of showing repentance, and Session’s contrary factual determination received great deference absent clear error, the later excommunication remained in effect.

The SJC found the appeal in order (17-4) and remanded the case for retrial (21-0) on grounds that the Judicial Commission committed significant procedural errors, including abandoning original charges and convicting Clark of contumacy on new charges without giving him opportunity to respond.

artifacts.synopsis: A complaint challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s approval of proceedings that cleared teaching and ruling elders without properly trying serious public accusations arising from Christ Church’s division. All three specifications were sustained because plea bargaining, dropped charges, and failure to hear necessary witnesses left the accusations unresolved. Presbytery’s action was annulled and de novo trials produced mixed convictions and acquittals. Harold Burkhart received six months’ suspension, Douglas McCready an admonition, and six former ruling elders three-month suspensions. The decision stressed taking such conflicts to Presbytery or judicial process rather than the congregation.
